To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
single-mode interferometers are more robust than multimode interferometers in all cases, and more ecient in all but low light cases, and even in these low light cases, the gain is limited to 20%.
multimode interferometry is always better in the low light regime and worse in the high light regime, and that the difference between both techniques is always less than 20% in any case.
single-mode interferometers are better than multimode ones in the high ux regime, and that multimode interferometers are better in low light levels.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the performance of groundbased interferometry in terms of phase estimation.
the development of a high-resolution, wide-eld imaging system for the purpose of monitoring the evolution of the solar atmosphere.
the performance of interferometric instruments, and more particularly with their sensitivity to the turbulence, in the case of ground-based interferometry.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
multimode interferometry is the best choice only when the light ux is very low, and the eld of view very large ( > 1 00 ), which is not the case for most of the current and upcoming interferometers.
single-mode interferometers have a higher performance than multimodes ones, except when the detector noise is dominant, and that the gain is signicantly higher in the high ux regime.
multimode interferometry is more robust to turbulence and detector noise, but that single-mode interferometer is more ecient in the high ux regime and in the fringe-tracking case.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
singlemode interferometry can be more robust than multimode interferometry, especially in the case of low light level and poor correction of the atmospheric turbulence.
, in most situations, single-mode interferometers should be preferred over multimode devices.
multimode interferometry is a better solution when the light is very weak, but that single-mode interferometers are more robust to the atmosphere and to the photon noise.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the choice of the interferometric scheme is more related to the application than to the light level.
single-mode interferometers can reach higher performance than multimodes ones when the correction provided to the atmospheric turbulence is poor.
single-mode interferometers should be considered as an option for the next generation of groundbased interferometers, especially for those aiming at high sensitivity and/or high spectral resolution.
